The migration from monolithic architectures to microservices involves three (3) primary considerations: (1) service decomposition strategy, (2) inter-service communication protocols, and (3) data consistency management. Each service should encapsulate a single bounded context (as defined in domain-driven design, or DDD). Communication between services typically utilizes either synchronous (e.g., REST, gRPC) or asynchronous (e.g., message queues, event streaming) patterns. The choice depends on latency requirements and fault tolerance thresholds. Data consistency presents the most significant challenge; traditional ACID transactions are generally infeasible across service boundaries. Instead, practitioners adopt eventual consistency models using the saga pattern (sometimes called long-running transactions). Monitoring is critical: each service must expose health check endpoints (typically HTTP GET /health) and emit structured logs (JSON format preferred). Container orchestration platforms (Kubernetes, abbreviated K8s) handle deployment, scaling, and self-healing. The total cost of ownership (TCO) increases initially but typically decreases at scale (approx. 18-24 months post-migration).
